Closed by Phase 11 sub-plan 11D Part 4 (11A Decision 6), by exactly the fix this row's own rationale named: `save-excursion' and `with-current-buffer' are prelude macros over Lisp `unwind-protect' in lisp/prelude.el, so no native frame stands between a `throw' in the body and a `catch' outside the form. Recorded by sub-plan 10D Part 1, after measuring the oracle rather than reading a manual. In GNU Emacs 31.0.90 a member of after-change-functions that signals is called exactly ONCE across three insertions: the error reaches the caller, Emacs empties the hook, and the later insertions are clean. kg contains the error, reports `Hook error (HOOK): MESSAGE' in the echo area, and leaves the member armed, so the same shape runs three times and reports three times -- which on a per-keystroke hook makes the buffer unusable rather than merely noisy. comparison is kg-policy because the two containment models are not comparable form for form: Emacs' disarming is a modification-hook rule specifically, while kg's containment is the mechanism that lets a C-g or a budget completion survive a hook (sub-plan 06E's protected call), and removing an entry from inside its own run would have to answer what happens to the rest of the list. Recorded, not fixed. A *package* can take Emacs' policy for itself, and the proof that it can is lisp/auto-fill.el: its hook entry point is a condition-case that stores the condition, remove-hooks itself and messages once, and the cited PTY case asserts the package's own line reaching a real screen while `Hook error' does not -- inverting the condition-case turns that case red with exactly the opposite pair.

`kill-buffer-hook', Phase 18. Emacs' ordering, taken deliberately: the hook runs IN the dying buffer, while it is still live, and only once every refusal has been passed -- kg calls it from the one point inside buf_kill_commit() after the lifecycle reservation succeeds, from which the kill can no longer fail. It is the only hook kg runs synchronously rather than off the event queue, and it has to be: kg's lifecycle events drain at the main loop's safe point, by which time the buffer is freed and its handle stale, so a hook run there could only be told that something died. TWO BOUNDS, both kg's and both tested: a hook body may not kill the buffer it is being run for (refused, because the commit that called it is still going to tear that slot down), and a nested kill runs no hook of its own. Killing another buffer, and therefore `with-temp-buffer' in a hook body, works -- at the ordinary event-ring cost prelude-with-temp-buffer records. Hook errors are contained and reported like every other hook's, so a broken kill-buffer-hook cannot wedge `C-x k'; the hook-error-does-not-disarm divergence applies here too.

`post-command-hook', Phase 18, landed on a measurement and divergent on its trigger. THE MEASUREMENT the plan demanded, from the counting build (test/perfobj/kg, $KG_PERF_OUT) over a 20-keystroke session: with an empty hook list post_command_hook_calls 24, post_command_hook_runs 0, arena free slots 46457, collections 0; with one small hook installed, calls 24, runs 24, free slots 46271 (186 slots for 24 invocations), collections 0. An unused hook therefore reaches fe zero times and allocates nothing -- what it costs a keystroke is one find_hook() string compare over a table that is empty -- which is the 'effectively zero' the plan made the condition for landing it. test_post_command_hook_empty_costs_nothing is the same shape as an assertion. THE DIVERGENCE is when it fires: Emacs runs it after each COMMAND, and kg runs it after each keystroke the main loop has finished processing. kg has no `self-insert-command' -- an ordinary character is inserted without going through cmd_invoke() -- so 'after each command' would leave typing out, and typing is the case a post-command hook is most often written for. The visible consequence is that a prefix keystroke that runs no command fires it too.

The Phase 18 follow-up: what a dynamic `let' over a buffer-local name restores INTO, once the answer is no longer 'whatever the value cell happens to be at exit'. Five shapes frozen against the oracle before the seam that closes them was written -- a `let' over the default left in a buffer that has a local binding, two `let's over one local left in another buffer, a throw out of such a form, the displaced buffer killed inside the form, and the displaced local killed inside the form. They are the interactions the two divergences (phase18-let-buffer-switched-out, phase18-make-local-while-let-bound) do not pin on their own, and the two ways a saved value has to be DROPPED rather than written anywhere are the pair a naive fix gets wrong. All five agree, on the seam FE_API_VERSION 11 opened: the `let' carries the binding's identity as its tag, and the restore resolves it to a cell or to nothing. The two drops are Emacs' own -- `local-variable-p SYM WHERE' is what its unbind consults, and a killed buffer has no local variables and a killed local binding is not one, so neither saved value is written anywhere.

Recorded by sub-plan 10C (10A Decision 7 named it as an existing row; it was not one). Emacs' `load` searches `load-path`; kg's does not. A bare name resolves to exactly one place, <config>/kg/lisp/NAME.el, and a name containing '/' is a literal path -- `require` is the only form that searches, and it searches kg's bounded C-side load-path rather than a Lisp list. comparison is kg-policy because there is nothing to compare: the search list is a bounded array of 8 directories a package cannot push onto, and Emacs' probing order (.elc, .el, no suffix) has no kg analogue -- kg tries the one suffix, which since 10C both loaders agree on. The practical shape of the divergence: an init file that does (add-to-list 'load-path DIR) then (load "pkg") works in Emacs and fails here, while (add-to-load-path DIR) then (require 'pkg) works. Documented in README.md, doc/kg.1 and doc/lisp-api.md; the bounded array is a deliberate design (see src/lisp_require.c's header), not an unimplemented feature. The failure CONDITION for a name that resolves to nothing is Emacs' `file-missing' since Phase 12, with Emacs' own (OPERATION STRERROR PATH) data -- see the phase12-file-conditions row. What stays divergent here is the SEARCH, not the condition: this row is about where kg looks, and it is a bounded C-side array either way.

The C half of the Phase 12 fix-cycle loader rebuild (sub-plan 12D Part 2, completed by the fix cycle on fe's FE_API_VERSION 8 input-unit trio). `load' and `require' are prelude Lisp loops; these natives own what C must own. internal--load-begin opens a load stream -- whole file into the next state.load_buffers slot, cursor and per-slot path copy beside it (fe borrows the unit label for the unit's whole lifetime), FeEnterInputUnit with the path as label -- and either returns a fully-open stream or raises with nothing changed, so the prelude's unwind-protect never sees partial state. internal--read-form answers the next form as the one-element list (FORM), keeping end-of-input (nil) distinguishable from a form reading as nil, with the form's own line latched so a raise while `eval'ing it reports path:LINE of the form. internal--load-end leaves the input unit and frees the buffer; it runs from the prelude loop's unwind-protect, i.e. on every completion kind via fe's cleanup drain. Phase 15. kg's case conversion is ASCII-only: the editor carries no Unicode case tables and buying a pair of them for three functions is not a trade this phase makes. A byte >= 0x80 passes through unchanged, so the ASCII case agrees exactly and the non-ASCII case does not. A byte >= 0x80 does count as a word constituent for `capitalize', which is what keeps the ASCII letters of a non-ASCII word from each being read as the start of one: "elan" spelled with an accent capitalizes to itself here and to its own capitalization in Emacs -- one letter apart, not two words apart.

Answers the command registry's question. A NAME is a built-in cmdtable row or a defun whose body carried an (interactive ...) declaration; since Phase 19 a FUNCTION OBJECT is asked by identity, so (commandp (symbol-function 'my-command)) is t -- defun binds the closure once and hands the same object to the registry and to the function cell, which is what makes identity a real answer rather than a guess. What is left of the divergence, and all that is left: Emacs asks a function whether it CARRIES an interactive form, so an anonymous (lambda () (interactive) 1) is a command there and is not one here -- kg's `interactive` is an inert macro and a lambda carries no metadata. commandp-anonymous-lambda is that case, and it is why this row stays divergent; interactive-command-predicate is the half that agrees, and the function-object half is its own supported row (phase19-commandp-function-object), because a case that agrees may not sit in a divergent row -- the XPASS rule. The capture/restore pair sub-plan 11D Part 4 replaced internal--save-excursion and internal--with-current-buffer with. Those two were natives that called the body as a thunk, which is what made a `throw' out of the body uncatchable outside the form; the two forms are now prelude macros over Lisp `unwind-protect' and only the editor state stays in C. (internal--excursion-capture SAVE-POINT) answers a right-gravity marker at point in the current buffer when SAVE-POINT is non-nil and the current buffer object when it is nil -- the two scopes save-excursion and with-current-buffer respectively preserve, which are the scopes the natives preserved before and Emacs' own. (internal--excursion-restore STATE) puts it back and releases it, tolerantly: a buffer killed underneath the form is a restore with nothing to restore to, not an error, because an unwind-protect cleanup that raises REPLACES the completion it was unwinding and would swallow the error that killed the buffer. The saved state is a GC-managed adapter object rather than a malloc'd record with an fe cleanup registration, so an unwind that never reaches the cleanup cannot leak one. kg-policy: Emacs has no such pair, and what IS Emacs-comparable is the behaviour of the two macros built on them.

`setq-local''s worker, one call per SYMBOL VALUE pair. Phase 15. The escaped set is Emacs 31.0.90's own, measured character by character: `.', `*', `+', `?', `[', `^', `$' and backslash, and NOT `]' -- a `]' outside a bracket expression is an ordinary character in this dialect. Since Phase 12's fix cycle `require' itself is prelude Lisp sharing `load''s loop; the C half (resolve/push/pop/check, see loader-stream-natives) keeps the feature table, the cyclic-require stack and the did-not-provide verdict, and a `throw' out of a required file now reaches a `catch' around the (require ...) exactly as load-throw-reachability describes.
`setq-default''s worker: writes the default wherever it currently lives, which is the variable's own value cell unless the current buffer has a binding shadowing it.
The backward half of native-skip-chars-forward, sharing its parser and therefore its recorded gap: named character classes are not understood. The distance it answers is negative, as Emacs'.

Emacs' SPEC syntax minus the named character classes: `[:alpha:]' and its family are read as the ordinary characters they are made of. Everything else is measured against 31.0.90 and agrees -- a leading `^' negates (so "" skips nothing and "^" skips everything), `-' between two characters is a range, a backslash quotes the next character, and the comparison is over CODEPOINTS rather than bytes, so a spec naming a multi-byte character skips whole glyphs. A class table populated with a guess would be worse than a missing one, so the gap is recorded here instead. The set is bounded at 64 ranges and a longer spec raises rather than truncating.
Process filter and sentinel callbacks get their own guarded frame: an error or throw in a callback is contained and reported on the status line, leaving the main editor loop intact.

Re-classified from supported by sub-plan 10C (10A Decision 3), because the old classification could never be true: `string-length` does not exist in the pinned Emacs at all -- the snapshot on file is `void-function (string-length)` -- so a `supported` `comparison: emacs` row was asserting that kg agrees with an oracle that raises. kg's own answer is 3, and it is the right answer for kg: `string-length` is a kg native that counts codepoints, and every expectation in the cited kg_test was measured against Emacs 31's `length` on the same strings (the test file's own header comment), UTF-8 counting included. The honest row is therefore a divergence in vocabulary, pinned by a case whose oracle record is the void-function it must stay.

Phase 15's regex-from-Lisp seam. Verified directly against the pinned oracle: (string-to-char "") is 0 in GNU Emacs 31.0.90, not nil. kg's non-empty-string case (e.g. (string-to-char "abc") = 97) already agrees with Emacs; only the empty-string edge case diverges. Not fixed in this slice (scope discipline).

Phase 15. Everything Emacs reads, kg reads the same way -- including the two shapes that are NOT numbers to it, "0x10" and "inf", and the difference between "1." (the integer 1, which is integer syntax to the reader too) and "1.5". Phase 15. kg's case conversion is ASCII-only: the editor carries no Unicode case tables and buying a pair of them for three functions is not a trade this phase makes. A byte >= 0x80 passes through unchanged, so the ASCII case agrees exactly and the non-ASCII case does not. A byte >= 0x80 does count as a word constituent for `capitalize', which is what keeps the ASCII letters of a non-ASCII word from each being read as the start of one: "elan" spelled with an accent capitalizes to itself here and to its own capitalization in Emacs -- one letter apart, not two words apart.

Phase 16. (y-or-n-p PROMPT) is one key, rendered "PROMPT(y or n) ", answering t for y/Y and nil otherwise -- editor_confirm_yn()'s policy, which every C-level "(y/n)" question in the editor already has, now sharing one implementation (prompt_ask_yn(), src/prompt.c). Emacs' `load' answers t on success; kg answered nil until Phase 11 (11A Decision 5, one line in native_load). WHAT THIS CASE PINS IS THE ORACLE SHIM'S PER-FORM SCOPING, NOT THE LEAK, and it stays `divergent' after Phase 12 closed the leak. Rewritten at Phase 12's pin (12A Decision 6, the trap the fact audit found) because the Phase 11 text claimed the case measured kg's global marking, and it never did. The acceptance evidence is the two-file probe test_phase12_one_arg_defvar_file_scope, which loads a file A whose own `let' answers from-A and a file B whose `let' on the same name answers unbound, byte-for-byte the pinned Emacs' answer for the same two files. Closing that last probe means the marking becoming a lexical-environment entry, a different and larger design in fe_eval.c; doc/TODO.md carries it. The two-argument arity has no such gap: its mark is global in Emacs too.

Closed at Phase 12's pin by fe 95965f0, and this is the row it never had: Phase 11 carried the gap forward in prose (doc/TODO.md and the fix cycle's fe-upstream entry) without a manifest entry, so nothing ran it. The Phase 12 fact audit restated it broader and simpler than Phase 11 had. It is NOT "a cleanup that handles its own error clobbers the in-flight condition": a `condition-case' or `ignore-errors' established inside an `unwind-protect' CLEANUP never handled anything at all, drain or no drain -- `(unwind-protect 'body (ignore-errors (car 6)))' was `body' in Emacs 31.0.90 and escaped to the host in kg, with nothing being unwound. The seam was one ordering in fe/fe_eval.c: RaiseCompletionCore tested ctx->cleanup_catch and replayed to RunOneCleanupEntry's setjmp before it ever called FindConditionHandler, so while any cleanup entry ran, every raise took that jump unconditionally. The fix accepts a found handler only when its frame index is at or above the floor RunOneCleanupEntry already saved for the current entry, which is why a NATIVE cleanup -- kg has three, and they do not republish run_base -- is bit-identical to before: nothing is above its floor, so no handler is ever accepted for it. WHAT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CHANGE is 06A Decision 4, measured correct against Emacs on every probe OF THE UNHANDLED-REPLACEMENT RULE ITSELF -- where the replacement is DELIVERED diverges in two pre-existing shapes, found post-close and pinned by the cleanup-raise-residuals row below and pinned here by the last two cases: an UNHANDLED cleanup raise still replaces the completion being unwound and is caught by the ENCLOSING handler, and a cleanup that throws still abandons the error. catch/throw inside a cleanup already worked, since only the condition-handler search was short-circuited.

Sub-plan 12D Part 2, and the item the Phase 12 fact audit found already half-built: `file-error' has been a row of fe's condition_parents[] since Phase 6 and has always been catchable from kg, so doc/TODO.md's claim that this needed "condition subtypes with an inheritance test in fe's handler search" was stale. `file-missing' under it is ONE DATA LINE (fe b030d0a), and it is what makes (signal 'file-missing ...) legal at all, since IsConditionSymbol gates `signal'. Exactly two kg sites raise it, both measured against Emacs 31.0.90 and both now byte-identical in class and data: the loader's cannot-open (src/lisp_io.c's read_whole_file) and `require' finding nothing in the load-path (src/lisp_require.c's resolve_require_path). The data is Emacs' uniform (OPERATION STRERROR PATH) triple of strings, with the FEATURE in the path slot for require, where nothing resolved. Everything else those two files raise is a kg-policy resource or limit error with no Emacs counterpart -- load depth, load-path full, out of memory, cyclic require, did-not-provide -- and stays a plain `error'. The loader's cannot-READ site also stays a plain `error', but NOT for lack of a counterpart: Emacs answers (file-error "Cannot open load file" "Is a directory" PATH) for (load DIRECTORY), measured on 31.0.90, so a (file-error ...) handler catches there and not here. Out of scope per 12A Decision 1, recorded so the next reader looks. TWO THINGS RECORDED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. (1) `permission-denied', Emacs' third file-error leaf: measurable only unprivileged, since chmod 000 is defeated by running as root, and this box runs the suite as root (12A Decision 1). kg raises the PARENT class, `file-error', for EACCES and nothing else, which is where a handler naming file-error catches it in either dialect. The split is on EACCES rather than on ENOENT because that was measured: a path whose parent is not a directory is ENOTDIR to kg's fopen and "No such file or directory" to Emacs, whose loader probes suffixes and answers its own not-found -- and it is file-missing on both sides (phase12-file-missing-not-a-directory). (2) The message. fe's `signal' uses the bare condition NAME as the completion message, so this change would have replaced kg's `cannot open PATH: No such file or directory' with the word `file-missing' and dropped the file name out of every diagnostic. render_file_condition() in src/lisp_core.c renders these two classes the way Emacs' error-message-string does instead -- `Cannot open load file: No such file or directory, /nope/x.el' -- rebuilt from the condition object rather than from state a raise would have to keep armed across a handler that catches it. The match is byte-for-byte for the (OPERATION STRERROR PATH) triple of strings -- the only shape kg's own raises produce -- including Emacs' rule that an empty OPERATION drops its `: ' separator; user-built shapes outside the triple (wrong arity, a non-string field) fall back to fe's own text by design. A general renderer for every condition is fe's `error-message' property, which neither tree has; this is the narrow version for the classes kg raises this way.

kg's `let' macro normalises its binding list and hands it to fe's core bindings-list `let'. Until Phase 11 it expanded to an immediate lambda application instead, which is why a `let' over a `defvar'd name was lexical: a lambda parameter is a lexical environment entry unconditionally, in fe and -- measured -- in Emacs 31 too, so the special flag is consulted at fe's binding-list paths and nowhere else (11A Decisions 2-3). The five dynamic cases here are the 11A grid's `let' half: nested extents (A3a), `setq' inside a binding writing the binding and not the value it hides (A2a), a closure reading the value in force when it is CALLED (A5), and the restore running on a throw (A6a) as well as on an error (A6b). The last two cases are guards, not targets: a defun parameter named after a special stays LEXICAL (A4), and a name no `defvar' ever named stays lexical under `let' (A13). An implementation that made every `let' dynamic would pass every target case here and fail both guards. The macro was not deleted outright, which 11D Part 2 proposed, because fe's core form raises wrong-type-argument for the one-element binding (a) where Emacs -- and kg before this change -- answers nil for (let ((a)) a); normalising in the macro keeps that, and keeps (let ((a 1 2)) a) answering 1, kg's long-standing reading of a shape Emacs rejects. A prelude macro over Lisp `unwind-protect' since sub-plan 11D Part 4, where it was a wrapper around the internal--save-excursion native before. The change of shape is what made a `throw' out of the body reach a `catch' outside the form (the catch-throw-reachability row); the state preserved is unchanged -- the current buffer and point in it, held by a right-gravity marker, so text inserted before the saved point carries it along. kg-policy because the state kg has to preserve is kg's; what is Emacs-comparable is the control flow through it, which the catch-throw-reachability and condition-case rows own. Two consequences of the macro shape are recorded rather than fixed, both found by the Phase 11 acceptance review. (1) The saved state is bound to the prelude temporary internal--excursion, so a body that ASSIGNS that name makes the cleanup raise -- and a raising cleanup replaces the completion it is unwinding (fe 06A Decision 4, which is Emacs' rule too), so the body's own error is lost: (condition-case e (save-excursion (setq internal--excursion nil) (error "MY-ERROR")) (error e)) answers the restore's type error, not MY-ERROR. It was the 11A Decision 3 capturable-temporaries exposure with a sharper consequence than the other names, and Phase 14's gensym closed it; the prelude-temporary-hygiene row is the rest of that sweep. (2) The saved marker is an adapter pool object, so the restore RELEASES its record rather than waiting for the collector; without that the 65th save-excursion between two collections raised the pool's exhaustion error, which is what the review's blocker was. test_save_excursion_pool_bound and two PTY cases pin it. THE POOL IS NO LONGER WHAT BOUNDS NESTING. Sub-plan 12D Part 3 raised LISP_MAX_OBJECTS 64 -> 256 (12A Decision 5), which costs 88 bytes a record -- +16.5 KB of .bss, 332392 -> 349288 -- and zero scc, and the binding constraint on nested save-excursion became fe's evaluation frame limit instead: re-measured on the finished tree, 218 nested forms answer and the 219th raises `evaluation frame limit exceeded', which is the same 1095-frame arena partition `with-current-buffer' has always lived under (155 deep, 156 raising, unchanged). At 64 the 65th nested form raised. Emacs has no pool bound at all -- 200000 live markers and a million sequential excursions run, and its first ceiling is the C stack at about 50000 nested -- so this is kg narrower by design, three orders of magnitude closer than it was. COLLECTOR BACK-PRESSURE WAS MEASURED AND REJECTED rather than left unbuilt: at the nesting threshold every record is LIVE, so a forced full collection frees exactly zero and the next allocation still fails -- the audit proved it by bursting 40000 conses inside the 64th nested excursion -- and it would have cost a new fe entry point and a second pin move to fix a different bug (dropped garbage). A realloc'ing pool is ruled out by construction: records are addressed by pointer inside their FeTFex0 wrappers and kg registers no mark_fn, so nothing could fix the pointers up after a move. The marker mint's exhaustion message said "too many buffer objects" until the same slice; it says "too many marker objects" now, which is what every measurement of this bound actually prints.

The sweep doc/TODO.md's capturable-temporaries row asked for, finishing what phase14-gensym-hygiene-in-prelude started on one name. Since Phase 11 a `let' over a `defvar'd name binds DYNAMICALLY, so any lisp/prelude.el temporary that is still bound while USER code runs is a two-way capture: the callback's assignment lands on the prelude's accumulator and the prelude's accumulator is what the user's variable reads back. Sixty distinct names are `let'-bound in the prelude (counted with utils/forecast_audit.py's reader); twenty-two binding sites across fourteen definitions are live across user code and were swept, and the rest bind and unbind with no callback in between, so nothing can observe them. Three classes were found rather than the two the exposure was recorded as: higher-order functions (mapcar, mapc, mapconcat, replace-regexp-in-string with a function REP, sort/internal--merge/internal--merge-pairs, seq-filter, seq-find, seq-some), the loader (internal--load-loop and require, which hold temporaries across the `eval' of a loaded file's forms), and one that is neither -- add-to-list, whose VARIABLE argument is a name the caller chose, so asking it to push onto a variable named `current' bound a shadow, read the shadow and `set' the shadow. Every case above raised or answered wrongly before and agrees with the pinned Emacs after; the kg_test carries the loader half, which needs a file on disk. THE FIX IS NOT GENSYM AND THE MEASUREMENT IS WHY. A macro substituting a fresh gensym through each body at load time was implemented first and works, but kg's arena is fixed and collects nothing during startup, so the substitution walk's own cost is permanent high-water mark: peak live after the prelude went 11281 -> 40153 objects of 56259 with a copying walk (20.0% -> 71.4%) and 11281 -> 20906 (37.2%) with a destructive one that allocates nothing itself, both measured at kgbatch -g's post-prelude probe. Carried into test_lisp.c's Phase 8 census, whose margin assertion is peak_live * 3 < total_slots and whose measured figure is 14579, that +9625 alone puts the census past a third of the arena. The cost is fe's call overhead -- about nine object slots per call, one call per cons -- not the copy. The temporaries are LAMBDA PARAMETERS instead, bound by an immediately-applied lambda, which fe binds lexically unconditionally (the special flag is consulted at fe's binding-list paths and nowhere else, 11A Decision 2 -- it is the pre-Phase-11 lowering of `let', used deliberately where hygiene is the requirement). Measured cost of that: peak live 11281 -> 11285, +4 objects, and prelude load 2.811 -> 2.810 ms, median of nine runs of the counting build each way.

Emacs' re-`defvar' rule comes with it and is measured: the value is not reassigned and the docstring IS replaced. `defcustom' inherits it by expanding to `defvar'. kg's registry (`internal--docs') still records the same string, because `apropos' asks `documentation' for a line about any name and the property is the only half Emacs has. A prelude macro over get-buffer-create + with-current-buffer + unwind-protect + kill-buffer, as the plan specifies. Three details are kg's and each is forced, and none of them is observable as a value: the buffer's NAME carries a gensym suffix, because kg has no generate-new-buffer and a fixed name would make a nested use reuse the buffer it is already inside; the cleanup clears the modified flag first, because kg's kill-buffer refuses a modified buffer rather than asking; and the kill is wrapped in ignore-errors, because a cleanup that raises REPLACES the completion it is unwinding, which would lose the body's value. That last one has a measurable bound: kg refuses a kill when the editor's lifecycle event queue is full, the queue drains once per keystroke, and each temp buffer costs three of its 64 slots -- so one command that opens more than about twenty temp buffers starts leaking them rather than failing.

The parent plan's §14 Proof 3: a small higher-order package whose pure-language portions also run unchanged under Emacs 31. lisp/pipeline.el is that pure portion -- no buffer, window, key or process -- and lisp/pipeline-text.el is the editor-facing half that (require ...)s it, which is also §14's 'multiple files' bullet. The nine cases here are the measurement, not the claim: each one's setup loads the tracked lisp/pipeline.el on BOTH sides and the snapshot is the pinned Emacs 31.0.90's own answer, so `make lisp-oracle-check' fails the moment the two stop agreeing. Between them they cover every §14 bullet: Lisp-2 cells, closures, funcall, apply, catch/throw, condition-case, one-step and fixpoint macro expansion used reflectively (10B's primitives, 10A Decision 2), macro expansion used as a predicate, and the macros evaluated normally. Two of kg's then-recorded silent divergences were deliberately NOT made load-bearing in the pure file, which is what makes the agreement a property rather than a coincidence: nothing rebinds a defvar'd variable around a call (prelude-defvar), and no returned value contains a (quote X) form (writer-quote-abbreviation). Both of those closed in Phase 11 and are `supported' now, so nothing here depends on them either way; the file is left as written because what it took to make the agreement a property is the record worth keeping. Two measured constraints shaped it: a throw could not cross a native re-entry boundary (catch-throw-reachability, also closed in Phase 11 for exactly the two forms this package avoids, though every other native re-entry is still a wall), so every catch and its throws are inside one function with no wrapping native between them; and `load' resolves a bare name only in the config directory (load-path-search), which is the one of the four that still diverges, so the two files reach each other with `require'.

Closed by Phase 11 (11A Decision 4, implemented in fe sub-plan 11C and inherited at 11D's pin); recorded as a divergence by 10C before that. Emacs' printer abbreviates a two-element (quote X) list back to 'X -- prin1, %S, the echo area, error renderings, all of them -- and fe's writer now does the same, recursively, so (format "%S" (list 'quote 'x)) is "'x" and (format "%S" (list 'a ''b 'c)) is "(a 'b c)" on both sides. The implementation is the symmetric copy of the (function f) -> #'f block that has been in WriteObject since Phase 4, with the same discrimination measured against the pinned Emacs: exactly one element after the head and the form proper, so (quote x y), (quote) and (quote . x) all keep printing as the pairs they are. Reading 'x produces that same two-element list on both sides, which is what made this the printer's gap and not the reader's. The sibling row phase8-reader-backquote-symbol-names records the neighbouring gap for backquote, which stays open and is different in kind: fe reads ` as `quasiquote' where Emacs reads it as a distinct symbol, so closing it means changing the reader's expansion symbols and breaking any Lisp that pattern-matches on quasiquote (11A Decision 4 rejects it by scope).
